An attempt is sometimes made to replicate findings of previous studies, but sometimes researchers alter methods slightly, not necessarily deliberately, leading to a change in results. A classic example of this is explained by Noah et al. (2018) on the facial feedback effect. Furthermore, researchers can feel pressured to obtain significant results, or findings consistent with their hypothesis. If this does not happen, results may not be published, despite them contradicting findings of earlier studies and providing insight into the topic. Though it is (hopefully) less common practice now, some researchers have been known for 'p-hacking,' or to use a very small or large sample size, then stop collecting data as soon as their results are significant. Therefore, as these results may not be accurate, it is important to replicate studies with different participants. The point is, if researchers' results aren't significant in the first place, the findings are less likely to be published, meaning some researchers always strive for a significant result, even if that means having a small sample size etc. It is only recently professionals have read papers and considered replicating studies of which the findings don't 'add up.' However, to replicate a study EXACTLY can be difficult, and to get a non-significant result published can be even harder.
